title: Occasional transport bridges hundreds of miles but not distant continents

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Occasional transport bridges hundreds of miles but not distant continents

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Occasional means of transport (sea currents, birds, drift timber, icebergs) suffice to carry organisms across a few hundred miles of sea, between islands or from a continent to a nearby island, but not between distant continents, so the floras of distant continents remain distinct.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: These means, however, would suffice for occasional transport across tracts of sea some hundred miles in breadth, or from island to island, or from a continent to a neighbouring island, but not from one distant continent to another.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XI, “Geographical Distribution”; section “Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means”. Scope: plants (and by extension other organisms) dispersing across seas

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch11-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Distance decay and colonization histories are testable in many island systems. Attribution to Darwin's listed vectors and a universal distance cutoff remain only partly identifiable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate successful natural colonization rates across ocean distances using island floras, dated phylogeographies, currents, bird movements, and organismal dispersal traits. Test for a steep decline after hundreds of miles and near-zero exchange between distant continents.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Rare long-distance events are hard to estimate from present ranges.

Human introductions contaminate modern distributions.

Observed disjunctions rarely identify the transport mechanism.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.61
data adequacy: 0.57
data existence: 0.82
discriminating power: 0.48
operationalizability: 0.69

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Floristic similarity against sea distance is computable from open checklists and can show whether distant continents are more distinct than nearby island gaps. That pattern is compatible with occasional short-range transport and also with old geology and trade. The data resolve the biogeographic outcome more readily than which means of transport produced it.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Plot floristic similarity against ocean distance and ask whether similarity remains appreciable over a few hundred miles, including continent-to-nearby-island gaps, and falls to the level seen between distant continents. Ready floristic exchange between distant continents would count against the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Currents, birds, driftwood, and ice are bundled together and are not separate variables in flora data.

Ancient land connections and human transport can produce the same distance decay.

fields.label: Dimension scores

data existence: 0.75
